what: Reversible compound pendulum — Kater principle. A reversible compound pendulum. One motor briefly moves the support of a separate rigid body and then holds. Rehang the same body from a different stock hole and compare the free-swing period. The paired suspension distances are unequal; a third pivot provides a physical comparison. A brief motor pulse moves a support and releases a passive rigid pendulum. Rehang the same body at its unequal paired pivot and compare periods; then test a third suspension with the same parts and program.
try: Load the model, press Reset, then Run. After a 1 s hold, the support moves to +8°, waits 0.12 s, returns to 0° and holds for 22 s. Watch the passive pendulum during that final hold.
Count complete swings from one crossing of the downward position to the next crossing in the same direction. Do not use a half-swing or the motor encoder as the period.
Predict what turning the same body over and hanging it from the paired hole will do. Load samebeat-conjugate.ldr, reset and repeat with the same program.
Repeat with samebeat-control.ldr. Compare its period, its swing amplitude and the held support position with the paired cases.
why: A rigid body has distributed mass. Its small-angle period depends on the ratio of rotational inertia about the pivot to the gravitational restoring torque. Two unequal pivot-to-centre distances can give the same ratio when their product equals the central moment of inertia divided by the total mass. This is conjugate suspension. A third pivot changes that balance even though the body and input program stay the same.
matters: Henry Kater used this principle in 1817 to measure gravity: he adjusted two knife edges on one bar until the periods matched, then the distance between them was the effective length, and g = 4π²L/T² followed without knowing the centre of mass. In the simulator this body, hung from holes 23.8 mm and 40.2 mm from its centre of mass, swings with periods of 0.50760 s and 0.50759 s. The predictions use the simulator's own masses and shapes; a real gravity measurement would need calibration.
question: Can hanging the same body from a hole closer to its centre of mass make it swing more slowly? Why might two unequal suspension distances have nearly the same period?
answer: Yes. Near the centre of mass the restoring torque becomes weak, while the body retains rotational inertia. The period depends on d + k²/d, where k² = I_G/M. Two unequal positive distances d1 and d2 give the same ideal small-angle period when d1*d2 = k². Equal periods alone do not establish conjugacy if the two distances are simply equal.
further: Compare the exact prepared-body predictions with periods measured from actual passive motion. Keep the source prediction separate from the measurement.
Inspect the swing amplitudes. Finite swings are slightly slower than the infinitesimal-amplitude limit, so different amplitudes can create a small period difference.
Compare Pendulum Array, which changes the lengths and mass distributions of three different arms. Here the rigid body is the same and its suspension changes.
A physical Technic bearing has friction and play. The supplied numerical experiment does not establish a precision gravity instrument.
formula: T0 = 2π sqrt[(I_G + M d²)/(M g d)] = 2π sqrt[(d + k_G²/d)/g], k_G²=I_G/M. For unequal conjugate distances d1*d2=k_G². For collinear opposite-side pivots, D=d1+d2 and T0=2π sqrt(D/g). Finite amplitude A in radians: T/T0≈1+A²/16.
